title: Orchestration: Pipelines as DAGs
summary: Why pipelines are modeled as directed acyclic graphs, how an orchestrator decides run order and parallelism, and how retries and upstream-failure states keep partial failures contained.
takeaways: A DAG encodes 'B needs A' as an edge. No cycles means there's always a valid run order.
A topological sort gives a run order. Grouping by depth shows what can run in parallel.
Retries absorb transient failures. Tasks should be idempotent so retrying is safe.
A failed task marks its descendants upstream_failed, and independent branches keep going.

steps.label: Parse DAG
steps.detail: Validate that every upstream exists and that there are no cycles.

steps.label: Find ready tasks
steps.detail: Tasks whose upstreams all succeeded. Initially, those with no upstreams.

steps.label: Run + retry
steps.detail: Execute. On an exception, retry up to max_retries times.

steps.label: Propagate state
steps.detail: Success unblocks downstream tasks. Failure marks descendants upstream_failed.

steps.label: Finish
steps.detail: Repeat until no runnable tasks remain, then report every task's state.

terms.definition: Directed acyclic graph: tasks as nodes and dependencies as edges, with no cycles.
A sequence of all nodes in which every node comes after all of its upstream dependencies.
Topological sorting by repeatedly removing nodes with no remaining incoming edges. Leftover nodes indicate a cycle.
An Airflow task state for tasks that didn't run because a dependency failed.
Re-running a failed task automatically, to absorb transient errors like network timeouts.
